newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to call at UN for reduction in greenhouse gases.
newsitem.headline: EU to call at UN for reduction in greenhouse gases.

text.p: The European Union will go to the United Nations' Earth Summit follow-up meeting next week seeking sharp reductions in greenhouse gases and a renewed commitment to sustainable development.

EU environment ministers, working on a joint position for the 15-nation bloc to present at the summit, are calling for a legally binding commitment for a 15 percent worldwide reduction in carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases from 1990 levels.
Such gases are blamed for global warming and the resultant climate change.
A special session of the U.N. General Assembly will be held on June 23-27 in New York bringing together as many as 70 world leaders to discuss progress made since the Earth Summit five years ago.

The Earth Summit, formally called the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, was held in June 1992 in Rio de Janeiro. It agreed two treaties -- one on climate change and one on protecting the world's plants and animals.

It was also intended to be a pact between North and South, the rich and developing worlds, in which the poorer countries would protect their environment as they grew in exchange for help from the rich in developing.
But little help has been forthcoming, in part because of the United Nations' own financial problems, leaving the EU worried that the poorer countries will give up on the process.

"From a European perspective, it is (a matter of) trying to to keep the developing countries on board, while trying to get the Americans on board," said Tony Carritt, European editor of Environment Watch newsletter.

Carritt said the EU sees itself as a bridge between the poorer countries, which fear that environmental concerns will stifle development, and the developed world which fears the impact of a massive burst of growth in the Third World.

The United States was widely viewed as the spoiler at the Rio summit, insisting on watering down the climate change treaty and refusing to sign the biodiversity pact on plants and animals which it then saw as threatening its biotechnology industry.
U.S. President Bill Clinton's administration, like its predecessor, remains reluctant to sign up to firm goals and timetables for the reduction of greenhouse gases.
Although the EU will go to the New York meeting -- which Clinton has now said he will attend -- there is little expectation that its call for 15 percent reductions will be heeded.
Another issue facing the follow-up meeting is whether to begin negotiations on a treaty to protect the world's forests.
The EU is keen for talks to begin on the treaty, which the Earth Summit deferred five years ago.
